explanations.answer: The words of his own mouth
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writer says the son has been "…trapped by the words of your lips, ensnared by the words of your mouth…" (Proverbs 6:2). No bandit, no ambush. Just a promise that left his own mouth and came back with teeth.

explanations.answer: A thief hiding by the road
explanations.explanation: No thief in this one, friend. The writer says the son was "…trapped by the words of your lips, ensnared by the words of your mouth…" (Proverbs 6:2). The trap was his own promise. Nobody had to jump out of the bushes.

explanations.answer: A debt his father left him
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse mentions a debt from his father, friend. The writer says the son has been "…trapped by the words of your lips, ensnared by the words of your mouth…" (Proverbs 6:2). It's the pledge he made himself that has him stuck. I wish it were somebody else's mess, but I think that's the sting of it.

That's the word, baker. The writer says, "Go, humble yourself, and press your plea with your neighbor." (Proverbs 6:3). It's not the easy road. I've had to swallow my pride once or twice, and it goes down like a dry cookie. But it gets the job done.

Nice try, friend, but a lawyer's speech isn't what the verse says. The writer says, "Go, humble yourself, and press your plea with your neighbor." (Proverbs 6:3). The word in the blank is humble. Defend isn't in the verse.

Excuses are easy to bake up, friend, and they come out flat every time. The writer says, "Go, humble yourself, and press your plea with your neighbor." (Proverbs 6:3). The word in the blank is humble. Excuse isn't in the verse.

Careful, friend, it's the other way around. The writer says, "Allow no sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids." (Proverbs 6:4). He doesn't say sleep on it. He says move now, and don't even get comfortable.

Right, baker. Nothing in the text says it can wait. The writer says, "Allow no sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids." (Proverbs 6:4). Not a nap, not a little shut-eye, none of it. The pillow will have to wait.
That's it, friend. The writer says, "Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise." (Proverbs 6:6). A tiny bug with a big résumé. Somebody get that ant a chef's hat.

Close, because locusts do show up in the Bible (Exodus 10:4), but not here. The writer says, "Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise." (Proverbs 6:6). The ant is the teacher in this passage. Locusts can sit this one out.

Good guess, friend, since the rock badger is a Bible animal too (Leviticus 11:5). But in this passage the writer says, "Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise." (Proverbs 6:6). The ant takes the teacher's chair here. The rock badger will have to wait for another day.

You've got it, baker. The writer says the ant works "Without a commander, without an overseer or ruler…" (Proverbs 6:7). No boss, no clipboard, no whistle. It just gets the work done. That's a better work record than mine.

This one flips it around, friend. The writer says the ant works "Without a commander, without an overseer or ruler…" (Proverbs 6:7). Nobody is standing over it giving orders. It gets the job done anyway, and that's the whole point.
Yes, baker. The writer says the ant "…prepares its provisions in summer; it gathers its food at harvest." (Proverbs 6:8). It packs the pantry while the getting is good. Smart little thing.

Winter isn't the season the verse names, friend. The writer says the ant "…prepares its provisions in summer; it gathers its food at harvest." (Proverbs 6:8). Summer and harvest are the times the verse gives, and nobody is making the ant do it.

Spring is a fine season, but it's not named here. The writer says the ant "…prepares its provisions in summer; it gathers its food at harvest." (Proverbs 6:8). The verse has the ant preparing in summer and gathering at harvest. Planting isn't mentioned.

Good thinking, but not quite. The warning isn't one big sleep. It's "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest…" (Proverbs 6:10). Little, little, little. It sneaks up like that.

That's right, friend. The writer doesn't warn about one long snooze. He says, "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest…" (Proverbs 6:10). Every one of those is little. They sound harmless, and I think that's the danger.

Yes, baker. The writer says, "…poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit." (Proverbs 6:11). That comes right after "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest…" (Proverbs 6:10). Little rests on one side, and poverty like a robber on the other.

Sickness is a real thing, friend, but it's not what the text says. The writer says, "…poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit." (Proverbs 6:11). Poverty is the word that fits the blank. The warning is about running short.

I can see why you'd guess shame, friend, but the text goes another way. The writer says, "…poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit." (Proverbs 6:11). Poverty is the one that fits the blank. It's the one that comes in like a robber.

explanations.answer: His eyes and feet and fingers
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. He is "…winking his eyes, speaking with his feet, and pointing with his fingers." (Proverbs 6:13). His mouth is perverse and the rest of him joins in. I'd say he's got a full-body conversation going on.

Nothing like that in the text, friend. The writer says he is "…winking his eyes, speaking with his feet, and pointing with his fingers." (Proverbs 6:13). No mail, no messengers. He does it all with his own body.

explanations.answer: Songs and riddles at the gate
explanations.explanation: Fun guess, but no songs and no riddles here, friend. The writer says he is "…winking his eyes, speaking with his feet, and pointing with his fingers." (Proverbs 6:13). It's all body language. Eyes, feet and fingers do the talking.
That's the word, friend. The writer says, "With deceit in his heart he devises evil…" (Proverbs 6:14). The winking and pointing are only what you see on the outside. The plan is inside.
Not fear, baker. The writer says, "With deceit in his heart he devises evil…" (Proverbs 6:14). The text puts deceit in his heart. Fear isn't in the verse.
Sorrow isn't the word here, friend. The writer says, "With deceit in his heart he devises evil…" (Proverbs 6:14). The word is deceit, and it's in his heart as he devises evil.
Right, baker. The writer says, "he continually sows discord." (Proverbs 6:14). Continually, so it's a habit and not a slip. That's on top of the evil he devises.
Panic's a good word, but it's not the one here. The writer says, "he continually sows discord." (Proverbs 6:14). Discord is the seed this man keeps scattering. Panic isn't in the verse.
Envy is a fair guess, friend, but not in this verse. The writer says, "he continually sows discord." (Proverbs 6:14). Discord is what he's planting, and the verse says he does it continually.

Yes, baker. The writer says, "…calamity will come upon him suddenly; in an instant he will be shattered beyond recovery." (Proverbs 6:15). Suddenly, in an instant. That's how fast the verse says it comes.

explanations.answer: A slow and quiet decline over time
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite, friend. The writer says, "…calamity will come upon him suddenly; in an instant he will be shattered beyond recovery." (Proverbs 6:15). Suddenly, in an instant. There's nothing slow about it.

There's no money talk in this verse, friend. The writer says, "…calamity will come upon him suddenly; in an instant he will be shattered beyond recovery." (Proverbs 6:15). What comes is calamity, and it comes fast.
Yes, baker. Right there in the list is "…a lying tongue…" (Proverbs 6:17). It's number two of the seven that are detestable to Him. The writer didn't hide it in the fine print.

It's on there, friend. The list says "…haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood…" (Proverbs 6:17). The lying tongue is right in the middle. The LORD hates it, according to the writer.

explanations.answer: Each one is a part of the body
explanations.explanation: Good eye, baker. Eyes, tongue and hands are all body parts (Proverbs 6:17). The list keeps going that way, with a heart and feet next (Proverbs 6:18). It's a whole person, head to toe, and the sins are in how each part gets used.

explanations.answer: Each one is a sin of the priests
explanations.explanation: Priests aren't mentioned anywhere in this list, friend. What the first three share is that each is a part of the body: eyes, tongue and hands (Proverbs 6:17). The writer keeps that going with a heart and feet (Proverbs 6:18). Look at the body parts and you've got it.

explanations.answer: Each one is a sin against parents
explanations.explanation: Parents don't show up in this list, friend. The first three are "…haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood…" (Proverbs 6:17). What they share is that each one is a part of the body. The list then goes on to a heart and feet (Proverbs 6:18).
That's it, baker. The writer says "…feet that run swiftly to evil…" (Proverbs 6:18). Fast feet headed the wrong way. Running is great, but not toward that.
Wandering isn't in the verse, friend. The writer says "…feet that run swiftly to evil…" (Proverbs 6:18). These feet run, and they run swiftly.
These feet aren't standing around, friend. The writer says "…feet that run swiftly to evil…" (Proverbs 6:18). They run, and they run swiftly. There's no gate in the verse at all.
